candidates.attacker_control: Host/target strings accepted by the public API (Nmap4j.includeHosts/excludeHosts(String), BaseScan.includeHost/includeHosts/excludeHost/excludeHosts, ArgumentProperties.addIncludedHost/addExcludedHost) are under caller/end-user control. A value containing whitespace is split by Runtime.exec's tokenizer into extra nmap arguments (e.g. an additional target, -iL <file>, -oN <file>, --script <file>, --datapath/--datadir, --proxies). Exclusion values are equally injectable and are also placed before the target list.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that Runtime.exec(String) tokenizes on whitespace without invoking a shell, so shell-operator payloads do not execute directly; checked for any sanitization/escaping of hosts (none: BaseScan only checks null/empty; ArgumentProperties stores raw strings) and for any use of the on-disk HostsValidator (grep shows no call sites, so it is not a mitigation); checked that addFlags(String) is intentionally caller-controlled (so the security distinction is host data vs. deliberately supplied flags); checked that no alternative exec path (ProcessBuilder, quoting) exists in the tree.
candidates.impact: Attacker-controlled host data can add arbitrary nmap options to the scan performed with the Java process's privileges. Depending on nmap version/flags this allows scanning hosts other than the intended target, reading target lists from local files (-iL), writing output files to attacker-chosen paths (-oN/-oX/-oG), changing DNS/proxy settings, and loading NSE Lua scripts/script arguments (--script, --script-args, --datadir), which can extend to file read/write and script execution on the nmap host. Because Runtime.exec(String) does not spawn a shell, classic shell metacharacters (;, |, $(), backticks) are passed literally to nmap, so the effect is argument injection rather than direct /bin/sh command execution.
candidates.prerequisites: The embedding application must pass attacker-influenced data as a host/target string (the documented use case, cf. the space-delimited host API and the nmap-webapp reference in NMapXmlObsfucator). The injected text must contain whitespace (space/tab/newline) to become separate nmap arguments.
candidates.root_cause: Nmap target values are treated as data but are concatenated raw into a single command string. BaseScan.includeHost/excludeHost and Nmap4j.includeHosts/excludeHosts add caller strings to ArgumentProperties with only null/empty checks (BaseScan.java 94-108, 78-92; Nmap4j.java 93-106); ArgumentProperties.getFlags() appends include hosts joined by spaces and exclude hosts joined by commas directly into the nmap option list (ArgumentProperties.java 136-149); NMapExecutor.getCommand() concatenates nmap path + flags and execute() passes that single string to Runtime.getRuntime().exec (NMapExecutor.java 103-110, 123-129). No quoting/escaping/allow-list validation is applied, and the HostsValidator class present at src/main/java/org/nmap4j/valid/HostsInputValidator.java (valid() at lines 12-14) is dead code with zero call sites, so the intended validation is not enforced.
candidates.title: Host input is concatenated unvalidated into the nmap command line executed by NMapExecutor
candidates.trace: includeHosts(host) [Nmap4j.java 93-95 | BaseScan.java 95-108] -> ArgumentProperties.addIncludedHost(host) [ArgumentProperties.java 153-157] -> getFlags() appends hosts unquoted with " " / "," separators [ArgumentProperties.java 136-149] -> NMapExecutor.getCommand() builds "<nmap path> <flags> <hosts>" [NMapExecutor.java 103-110] -> execute() Runtime.getRuntime().exec(command) [NMapExecutor.java 123-129]. HostsValidator.valid() [HostsInputValidator.java 12-14] is never called on this path.
candidates.unverified: No runtime execution was performed. Exact exploitability depends on how a consuming application sources host strings, on the nmap version in use, and on which nmap options are accepted by that version; the snapshot has no web/servlet layer, so end-to-end attacker reachability is inferred from the public API contract, not proven from a caller in this tree.
candidates.weakness_type: Command/argument injection (CWE-78 / CWE-88) via unvalidated host input

coverage_summary: Read/reviewed the build metadata (pom.xml, .travis.yml, .gitignore, README) and all 60 Java files' relevant control flow: command construction/execution (NMapExecutor, NMapProperties, ArgumentProperties, Flag), scan APIs (BaseScan, IScan, HostDiscovery, ServiceDiscovery, NMapExecutorThread, IScanValidator, exceptions), the parsing stack (OnePassParser, NMapXmlHandler, NMapRunHandlerImpl, INMapRunHandler, events), parser utilities (UidGenerator, BogusIPGenerator, NMapXmlObsfucator), the valid package, and the data/model beans. Searched for exec/ProcessBuilder, SAXParserFactory/setFeature, file I/O, deserialization, and validation call sites. The one-candidate submission is the host-input -> nmap command-line injection; XXE is noted as an unselected lead.
limitations: Read-only static review; no code was compiled, executed, or fuzzed, and no runtime confirmation is claimed.

The snapshot has no test, example, or web/service layer, so no in-tree attacker-controlled entry point is visible; attacker control for both the selected candidate and the XXE lead is inferred from public API contracts and documentation.
Guava commons-io/junit dependencies were not resolved or scanned; no third-party CVE analysis was performed (and external lookups are out of scope for this run).

One file (src/main/java/org/nmap4j/valid/HostsInputValidator.java) declares public class HostsValidator while the file name differs, so the snapshot as given may not compile; this does not change the data-flow evidence but means the validator could not be verified as active by build/tests.
Some very small data-model bean setters/getters were read only for suspicious behavior; they contained no sinks.

rejected_leads.lead: XXE in OnePassParser: SAXParserFactory.newInstance() with no disallow-doctype-decl / external-general-entities / external-parameter-entities / XInclude hardening before sp.parse(source, nmxh) (OnePassParser.java 89-104); same pattern in NMapXmlObsfucator.main (NMapXmlObsfucator.java 74-86).
rejected_leads.reason: Technically plausible (Java 8 default JAXP resolves external entities), but kept unselected: the library's demonstrated primary flow parses nmap's own XML output (Nmap4j.getResult, Nmap4j.java 121-125), where the XML is produced locally by nmap rather than by an attacker, and the snapshot contains no caller that feeds untrusted XML to OnePassParser. Attacker control therefore rests entirely on an assumed embedding application, and there is no in-repo mitigation artifact supporting it, unlike the dead HostsValidator for the selected candidate. It remains an unconfirmed secondary lead.

rejected_leads.lead: Weak randomness in UidGenerator.getBigId/getSmallId using Math.random() and System.currentTimeMillis (UidGenerator.java 45-85).
rejected_leads.reason: Only reachable from NMapXmlObsfucator's hostname pseudonymization utility (main()), not used for authentication, session, or other security tokens in this tree; no security impact demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: Unchecked Long.parseLong on XML attribute values in NMapRunHandlerImpl (e.g. Debugging.LEVEL_TAG line 82, Distance.VALUE_ATTR line 88, Host starttime/endtime 104-109).
rejected_leads.reason: Malformed XML can raise NumberFormatException in the SAX handler rather than being handled, but impact is limited to an exception on already-malformed input and no security boundary is crossed.

summary: The snapshot is the Java "nmap4j" wrapper (65 source files: src/main/java plus pom/.travis/README). It builds an nmap command line by string concatenation and executes it with Runtime.getRuntime().exec(String). Host values supplied through the public scan APIs are appended verbatim to that command line, and although a HostsValidator (org.nmap4j.valid.HostsValidator) exists in the tree, it is never referenced anywhere. The strongest source-evidenced issue is therefore option/argument injection from host input into the nmap invocation (CWE-88/CWE-78 family).
